========== OUTPUT [patient] ==========
I don't... I mean, I don't really see it like that. It’s not about trying to control my life, because my life is already very, very structured just by the sheer nature of what I do. You have to understand, when you’re dealing with biological assays and cellular cultures, there is absolutely no room for error. The protocols are written down to the exact micro-liter, the exact temperature, the exact second. My life is already dictated by the science, if that makes sense. 

So it’s not that I’m using my meals to somehow feel like I'm the one in charge of everything else... it’s just that my eating habits have to fit into that pre-existing structure. If I have a twelve-hour incubation period, and I need to prep the next phase of the experiment at exactly hour six, I can't just drop everything, de-gown, wash up, and wander off because society says it's "lunchtime." People outside of research, like the occupational health people, they just don't really get it. They think, oh, just take a break, have a sandwich. But a break means potential contamination risks, it means losing your headspace, it means breaking the sterile field. 

Keeping my intake small and precise when I finally do get home... it’s just practical. It’s about not disrupting the workflow and not feeling horrible the next day. I don't sit there at night thinking, you know, "If I only eat this specific portion, I'm the master of my destiny." It’s much more pragmatic than that. It’s more like, if I eat a heavy meal, I’ll wake up with brain fog, or I won't sleep well, and I simply cannot afford brain fog when I’m analyzing this volume of data and trying to coordinate an entire departmental exhibition at the same time. 

And honestly, my life is fine. I don't feel out of control in a way that I'd need to compensate for. Our grant funding is secure for another eighteen months, the department head is thrilled with my progress, even if the exhibition is a massive time sink. So no, I really don't think it’s some deep psychological thing about seeking control over my existence. It’s just... efficiency. Pure and simple efficiency. I just don't understand why that's so hard for the university to grasp.

========== OUTPUT [patient] ==========
I wouldn't say I get anxious about the eating schedule itself, no. Because, well... I don't really have a "planned eating schedule" in the way I think you’re implying. My schedule is just... the lab’s schedule. If I can't stick to my usual routine, it usually means something has gone catastrophically wrong with the research. 

Like, just last Thursday, for example, we had this completely unexpected pressure drop in one of the clean rooms. Facilities has been ignoring the HVAC warnings for weeks, which is a whole other issue I've had to escalate to the dean, but suddenly I had to spend three hours recalibrating the environmental sensors and documenting the deviation for the compliance logs. During all that, did I stop to eat? Of course not. Was I anxious? Yes, absolutely, my heart was pounding, but I was anxious because months of delicate cellular growth were at risk of contamination, not because I missed some arbitrary window to have a meal! 

I just don't have this rigid food diary that I'm obsessing over. I just eat when the work is done, whenever that happens to be. If the work takes until nine at night, I eat at nine. If the exhibition planning keeps me at my desk until midnight—which it has been lately, because the catering people for the opening gala keep emailing me about dietary restrictions for the donors, which is incredibly tedious—then I eat at midnight. 

It’s really not upsetting to delay it. Honestly, it would be infinitely more upsetting to force myself to stop and eat when I know the centrifuge is running or the data hasn't been backed up. The only time I ever actually feel upset or, I guess, irritated about food schedules is when people like the university health board try to force me into *their* schedule. They want me to eat at noon. Noon is peak analysis time for my current assay! It just makes absolutely no logical sense to drop a pipette, de-gown, wash up, and go chew on something just because the clock struck twelve. It’s so arbitrary. So, no, I don't get upset about my own routine, because my routine is just a byproduct of doing my job correctly.

Well, yes, I suppose there has been a change. The occupational health nurse certainly made a massive fuss over the number on the scale when they forced me to do that intake physical last week. I'm keeping myself contained, you know? I'm not letting the stress turn me into someone who is sluggish or out of control. If I were getting soft, that would mean the department's disorganization was winning, and I simply cannot allow that to happen when I have a team of junior researchers relying on my data analysis. Just yesterday, my post-doc came to me in an absolute panic because she thought she'd cross-contaminated the control group, and if I hadn't been sharp and completely dialed in, we might have had to scrap three weeks of work. So, yes, my weight is lower, but it’s just a reflection of my dedication and my ability to stay unaffected by the mess around me. I really don't see why the university is treating it like a medical crisis when it's literally the thing keeping me anchored.

It's just easier, and much more efficient, to keep working. I need things to be exact, orderly, you know? Just a very specific, small amount so I can maintain my clarity. I mean, I don't really see it like that. It’s not about trying to control my life, because my life is already very, very structured just by the sheer nature of what I do. You have to understand, when you’re dealing with biological assays and cellular cultures, there is absolutely no room for error. The protocols are written down to the exact micro-liter, the exact temperature, the exact second. My life is already dictated by the science, if that makes sense. \n\nSo it’s not that I’m using my meals to somehow feel like I'm the one in charge of everything else... it’s just that my eating habits have to fit into that pre-existing structure. If I have a twelve-hour incubation period, and I need to prep the next phase of the experiment at exactly hour six, I can't just drop everything, de-gown, wash up, and wander off because society says it's \"lunchtime.\" People outside of research, like the occupational health people, they just don't really get it. They think, oh, just take a break, have a sandwich. But a break means potential contamination risks, it means losing your headspace, it means breaking the sterile field. \n\nKeeping my intake small and precise when I finally do get home... it’s just practical. It’s about not disrupting the workflow and not feeling horrible the next day. I don't sit there at night thinking, you know, \"If I only eat this specific portion, I'm the master of my destiny.\" It’s much more pragmatic than that. It’s more like, if I eat a heavy meal, I’ll wake up with brain fog, or I won't sleep well, and I simply cannot afford brain fog when I’m analyzing this volume of data and trying to coordinate an entire departmental exhibition at the same time. \n\nAnd honestly, my life is fine. I don't feel out of control in a way that I'd need to compensate for. Our grant funding is secure for another eighteen months, the department head is thrilled with my progress, even if the exhibition is a massive time sink. So no, I really don't think it’s some deep psychological thing about seeking control over my existence. It’s just... efficiency. Pure and simple efficiency. I just don't understand why that's so hard for the university to grasp.\n\nDoctor: Do you ever feel anxious or upset when you can't stick to your planned eating schedule?\n\nPatient: I wouldn't say I get anxious about the eating schedule itself, no. If I can't stick to my usual routine, it usually means something has gone catastrophically wrong with the research. \n\nLike, just last Thursday, for example, we had this completely unexpected pressure drop in one of the clean rooms. Facilities has been ignoring the HVAC warnings for weeks, which is a whole other issue I've had to escalate to the dean, but suddenly I had to spend three hours recalibrating the environmental sensors and documenting the deviation for the compliance logs. During all that, did I stop to eat? Of course not. Was I anxious? Yes, absolutely, my heart was pounding, but I was anxious because months of delicate cellular growth were at risk of contamination, not because I missed some arbitrary window to have a meal! \n\nI just don't have this rigid food diary that I'm obsessing over. If the exhibition planning keeps me at my desk until midnight—which it has been lately, because the catering people for the opening gala keep emailing me about dietary restrictions for the donors, which is incredibly tedious—then I eat at midnight. \n\nIt’s really not upsetting to delay it. They want me to eat at noon. Noon is peak analysis time for my current assay! So, no, I don't get upset about my own routine, because my routine is just a byproduct of doing my job correctly.\n\nDoctor: Have you noticed any significant changes in your weight over the past few months?\n\nPatient: Well, yes, I suppose there has been a change. I actually had to buy a new belt for my trousers recently because the ones I usually wear to the departmental meetings were practically falling off me, and even my standard-issue lab coats feel like they're swallowing me whole these days. Which, frankly, is a bit annoying because you really don't want loose fabric catching on a centrifuge latch or knocking over a rack of delicate micro-vials when you're moving around the bench... \n\nBut honestly? There is just so much absolute chaos at work right now—between the exhibition planning, the endless caterer emails, the HVAC failures in the clean room, the pressure to secure the next round of grant funding—it's just a constant, exhausting barrage of unpredictable variables. Every single day is a new crisis that someone else has caused and I have to fix. \n\nSo feeling that my clothes are loose, and knowing that I'm maintaining this strict efficiency... it just tells me that I’m not letting all that external chaos spill over into my body. I'm keeping myself contained, you know? I'm not letting the stress turn me into someone who is sluggish or out of control. If I were getting soft, that would mean the department's disorganization was winning, and I simply cannot allow that to happen when I have a team of junior researchers relying on my data analysis. Just yesterday, my post-doc came to me in an absolute panic because she thought she'd cross-contaminated the control group, and if I hadn't been sharp and completely dialed in, we might have had to scrap three weeks of work. So, yes, my weight is lower, but it’s just a reflection of my dedication and my ability to stay unaffected by the mess around me. I just don't understand why that's so hard for the university to grasp.\n\nDoctor: Do you ever feel anxious or upset when you can't stick to your planned eating schedule?\n\nPatient: I wouldn't say I get anxious about the eating schedule itself, no. Because, well... I don't really have a \"planned eating schedule\" in the way I think you’re implying. My schedule is just... the lab’s schedule. If I can't stick to my usual routine, it usually means something has gone catastrophically wrong with the research. \n\nLike, just last Thursday, for example, we had this completely unexpected pressure drop in one of the clean rooms. Facilities has been ignoring the HVAC warnings for weeks, which is a whole other issue I've had to escalate to the dean, but suddenly I had to spend three hours recalibrating the environmental sensors and documenting the deviation for the compliance logs. During all that, did I stop to eat? Of course not. Was I anxious? Yes, absolutely, my heart was pounding, but I was anxious because months of delicate cellular growth were at risk of contamination, not because I missed some arbitrary window to have a meal! \n\nI just don't have this rigid food diary that I'm obsessing over. I just eat when the work is done, whenever that happens to be. If the work takes until nine at night, I eat at nine. If the exhibition planning keeps me at my desk until midnight—which it has been lately, because the catering people for the opening gala keep emailing me about dietary restrictions for the donors, which is incredibly tedious—then I eat at midnight. \n\nIt’s really not upsetting to delay it. Honestly, it would be infinitely more upsetting to force myself to stop and eat when I know the centrifuge is running or the data hasn't been backed up. The only time I ever actually feel upset or, I guess, irritated about food schedules is when people like the university health board try to force me into *their* schedule. They want me to eat at noon. Noon is peak analysis time for my current assay! It just makes absolutely no logical sense to drop a pipette, de-gown, wash up, and go chew on something just because the clock struck twelve. It’s so arbitrary. So, no, I don't get upset about my own routine, because my routine is just a byproduct of doing my job correctly.\n\nDoctor: Have you noticed any significant changes in your weight over the past few months?\n\nPatient: Well, yes, I suppose there has been a change. The occupational health nurse certainly made a massive fuss over the number on the scale when they forced me to do that intake physical last week. I mean, I had already noticed that the numbers have kept drifting down over the last few months, it wasn't exactly a shock to me. And, practically speaking, my clothes are definitely looser. I actually had to buy a new belt for my trousers recently because the ones I usually wear to the departmental meetings were practically falling off me, and even my standard-issue lab coats feel like they're swallowing me whole these days. Which, frankly, is a bit annoying because you really don't want loose fabric catching on a centrifuge latch or knocking over a rack of delicate micro-vials when you're moving around the bench... \n\nBut honestly? Even though they see it as this huge red flag, a big part of me actually sees that downward drift as a positive thing. To me, it’s a sign that I’m focused. There is just so much absolute chaos at work right now—between the exhibition planning, the endless caterer emails, the HVAC failures in the clean room, the pressure to secure the next round of grant funding—it's just a constant, exhausting barrage of unpredictable variables. Every single day is a new crisis that someone else has caused and I have to fix. \n\nSo feeling that my clothes are loose, and knowing that I'm maintaining this strict efficiency... it just tells me that I’m not letting all that external chaos spill over into my body. I'm keeping myself contained, you know? I'm not letting the stress turn me into someone who is sluggish or out of control. If I were getting soft, that would mean the department's disorganization was winning, and I simply cannot allow that to happen when I have a team of junior researchers relying on my data analysis. Just yesterday, my post-doc came to me in an absolute panic because she thought she'd cross-contaminated the control group, and if I hadn't been sharp and completely dialed in, we might have had to scrap three weeks of work. So, yes, my weight is lower, but it’s just a reflection of my dedication and my ability to stay unaffected by the mess around me. I really don't see why the university is treating it like a medical crisis when it's literally the thing keeping me anchored.\n\n[Last Question]\nAre you afraid of gaining weight?\n\n[Patient Info]\n- demographics: Female / 40 / biological_scientist / graduate\n- severity: Moderate\n\n[Targeted Info]\nname: Fear_of_Weight_Gain\nmanifestation: \"If the scale goes up even a fraction, I feel this sharp panic that I’m losing the discipline I’ve worked so hard to maintain.\"\n\n[Conversation Style]\nYou are a Verbose patient.\nA verbose patient may\n1) provide excessively detailed responses when describing their symptoms and experiences, even when the details are directly relevant,\n2) elaborate extensively on the background, events, thoughts, feelings, and personal experiences surrounding their symptoms, and\n3) demonstrate difficulty allowing the doctor to guide the interview or move on to another clinical topic.\nThis is how you are, not a performance you put on in every reply — let it show as much or as little as the moment calls for.\n\nWhat to do:\n- Answer the doctor's last question with what [Targeted Info] holds, in your own words.\n- You are speaking out loud, not reading a line you prepared. ========== OUTPUT [patient] ==========
I wouldn't use the word "afraid," exactly, because that makes it sound like some sort of irrational phobia, like being afraid of the dark or something, which is just an evolutionary misfire. But... well, yes, I suppose there is a very intense reaction. It goes back to what I was just explaining about the absolute chaos I’m managing every single day. I have to keep myself so strictly regulated just to keep the department's work from collapsing in on itself. 

So, when I do check my weight—which I do track, of course, because I’m a researcher, I track all my personal metrics, it’s just second nature to log the data—if the scale goes up even a fraction, I feel this... this incredibly sharp panic. It just spikes right in my chest. Because to me, it means I’m losing the discipline I’ve worked so hard to maintain. 

It’s exactly like seeing an unexpected temperature fluctuation on the monitor for the minus-eighty degree freezers. You see that tiny shift in the numbers and you know instantly that the integrity of the system is compromised, that something has breached the protocol and years of samples are at risk. If my weight goes up, it means I’m getting sloppy. It means I’m letting the stress of the exhibition or the incompetence of the facilities team finally get to me, and I’m losing that tight, efficient control I need to function. It feels like the first crack in the dam. So yes, that sharp panic is very real, because if I lose my discipline, if I let myself get soft and sluggish, then I can't do my job. And there is simply no one else in the department who can step in and run these assays the way I do. I have to maintain the standard.

Ideal? I mean... I suppose "ideal" is a highly subjective metric, isn't it? If you're asking if I look at my physical baseline and think, "Yes, this is perfectly optimized," then... no, absolutely not. Not at all. 

I know everyone keeps telling me I’m so thin—the occupational health nurse with her little charts, my department head who keeps giving me these lingering, concerned looks during faculty meetings—but I just... I don't see it. I really don't see someone thin when I look at myself. 

Every morning, before I leave for the lab—which is usually around 5:30 AM, because I have to check the overnight incubation cultures before the undergrads get in and inevitably contaminate something—I get dressed, and I look in the full-length mirror in my bedroom. And despite all this supposed weight loss that the university is in such a panic over, I don't see a fragile person. I mostly just notice my stomach and my hips. They still just look... soft. They look entirely disproportionate to the level of efficiency I am operating at. 

And it is incredibly frustrating, because in my line of work, presentation and precision are everything. If I'm standing at the front of a lecture hall, or if I'm pitching a grant renewal to the oversight board, and I have this... this excess around my midsection or my hips, I feel like it makes me look completely careless. It makes me look unserious. Like I lack rigor. 

How can I expect a room full of post-docs or skeptical investors to trust my data validation if I look like someone who can't even manage her own physical parameters? It projects this image of sloppiness, of someone who is complacent and just lets things slide. And I am *never* complacent. I am the only person holding that lab together. But when I look in the mirror, those areas—the stomach, the hips—they just betray me. They make me look like someone who doesn't care about the details, which couldn't be further from the truth. So, no, my current weight isn't ideal. There is still entirely too much room for error, structurally speaking.

========== OUTPUT [patient] ==========
Well, if you’re asking if my actual output is suffering, the answer is absolutely not. I am still meeting all the main deadlines. The quarterly grant reports were actually submitted two days early, and the preliminary data for the exhibition is entirely on schedule, which is frankly a miracle given the sheer incompetence I’m dealing with on a daily basis. So my professional functionality is perfectly intact, I want to be very clear about that. 

But... I suppose, on a purely interpersonal level, yes, there has been a shift. I’ve completely stopped going to the lab lunches, for one thing. It used to be this whole Friday ritual where the entire department would order in from that heavy Italian place on the corner or the Thai restaurant, and... I just can't do it anymore. It’s an absolute nightmare of unquantifiable variables. You have no idea how much oil they’re cooking with, the portion sizes are absurd, and then you’re just expected to sit there for an hour, making idle chit-chat and eating all these heavy carbs while perfectly good bench time is just ticking away. 

And it’s not just the lab lunches. I’ve also had to bow out of all the informal gallery planning meals. The museum curators love to do these working dinners or meet for drinks and appetizers to discuss the exhibition layouts, which I find incredibly inefficient and honestly a bit unprofessional anyway. Why do we need to be consuming rich, unpredictable restaurant food just to decide on the placement of informational placards? It makes no sense. So, I’ve just been telling everyone I have to stay behind to monitor the incubators or run statistical analyses on the latest data sets. Which is true, I do need to do those things, but... 

The practical result is that I’m definitely more isolated from my colleagues than I used to be. I do realize that. I’ll see the post-docs and the junior faculty walking back from the breakroom laughing about some inside joke I’m not a part of, or I’ll find out they made some minor decision about the exhibition lighting over dinner without me because I wasn't there to weigh in. And I suppose it stings a little bit, feeling like I’m on the outside of my own team. I used to be right in the middle of all those conversations. But I just can't sit in those restaurants and participate in that... that mindless consumption. It completely disrupts my focus. And honestly, if being a bit isolated is the price I have to pay to maintain my discipline and keep this department from completely falling apart, then that’s just the cost of doing business. Someone has to stay sharp, right? I just can't afford to let my guard down over departmental pizza.

Eat more freely? I mean... I don't know if "freely" is a concept that even applies to my life or my schedule anymore. "Freely" implies a lack of structure, a lack of parameters, which is just a recipe for absolute chaos. It's not just about the weight, though obviously, as I just explained, maintaining my physical baseline and that structural integrity is paramount to my focus. But it's also about the sheer, unyielding logistics of my day-to-day operations. 

I suppose... well, I suppose occupational health sent me here to talk to you in the first place because they don't understand that. They just look at their standard nutritional guidelines and they panic, because I’ve gotten into this pattern where I push breakfast and lunch aside entirely during my lab runs. And I have to! If I'm doing a continuous multi-hour assay, or if we're in the middle of cataloging the delicate specimens for the new exhibition—which, by the way, has been an absolute nightmare because the climate control in the display cases keeps fluctuating and I am the only one monitoring it—I simply cannot stop to eat. 

So breakfast gets bypassed because I'm rushing in at dawn to check the incubators, and then lunch gets pushed aside because I'm elbow-deep in exhibition work or trying to fix whatever protocol the undergrads inevitably botched that morning. It's just so much more efficient to keep the momentum going. I can't break my concentration for a meal. 

And then, by the time I actually do stop to eat, usually late in the afternoon when the immediate fires are put out, I keep it to something very small and controlled. I have to. If I were to just eat "freely" or consume some large, unpredictable meal after running on high alert for ten hours, it would completely shock my system. It would make me sluggish, and I still have evening grant reports to file and data sets to review. So I have this very precise, very small amount that I allow myself, just enough to maintain my cognitive function without compromising my discipline or making me feel heavy and slow. 

But occupational health sees that—they see me skipping the cafeteria all day and then eating my meticulously portioned container at my desk at 4 PM—and they flag it as some sort of crisis. They see it as a problem to be fixed. But really, if I weren't worried about the weight or the discipline, I still don't think I could just eat "freely." How else am I supposed to manage all of this work if I don't maintain absolute control over every single variable, including what I take in?

But apparently, someone noticed my routine and decided it warranted a whole medical intervention, which is why I'm sitting here right now, even though I have a dozen samples waiting for me back at the lab that really need my attention...\n\nDoctor: Do you feel like controlling what and when you eat helps you feel more in control of other aspects of your life?\n\nPatient: I don't... I mean, I don't really see it like that. It’s not about trying to control my life, because my life is already very, very structured just by the sheer nature of what I do. You have to understand, when you’re dealing with biological assays and cellular cultures, there is absolutely no room for error. The protocols are written down to the exact micro-liter, the exact temperature, the exact second. My life is already dictated by the science, if that makes sense. \n\nSo it’s not that I’m using my meals to somehow feel like I'm the one in charge of everything else... it’s just that my eating habits have to fit into that pre-existing structure. If I have a twelve-hour incubation period, and I need to prep the next phase of the experiment at exactly hour six, I can't just drop everything, de-gown, wash up, and wander off because society says it's \"lunchtime.\" People outside of research, like the occupational health people, they just don't really get it. They think, oh, just take a break, have a sandwich. But a break means potential contamination risks, it means losing your headspace, it means breaking the sterile field. \n\nKeeping my intake small and precise when I finally do get home... it’s just practical. It’s about not disrupting the workflow and not feeling horrible the next day. I don't sit there at night thinking, you know, \"If I only eat this specific portion, I'm the master of my destiny.\" It’s much more pragmatic than that. It’s more like, if I eat a heavy meal, I’ll wake up with brain fog, or I won't sleep well, and I simply cannot afford brain fog when I’m analyzing this volume of data and trying to coordinate an entire departmental exhibition at the same time. \n\nAnd honestly, my life is fine. I don't feel out of control in a way that I'd need to compensate for. Our grant funding is secure for another eighteen months, the department head is thrilled with my progress, even if the exhibition is a massive time sink. So no, I really don't think it’s some deep psychological thing about seeking control over my existence. It’s just... efficiency. Pure and simple efficiency. I just don't understand why that's so hard for the university to grasp.\n\nDoctor: Do you ever feel anxious or upset when you can't stick to your planned eating schedule?\n\nPatient: I wouldn't say I get anxious about the eating schedule itself, no. Because, well... I don't really have a \"planned eating schedule\" in the way I think you’re implying. My schedule is just... the lab’s schedule. If I can't stick to my usual routine, it usually means something has gone catastrophically wrong with the research. \n\nLike, just last Thursday, for example, we had this completely unexpected pressure drop in one of the clean rooms. Facilities has been ignoring the HVAC warnings for weeks, which is a whole other issue I've had to escalate to the dean, but suddenly I had to spend three hours recalibrating the environmental sensors and documenting the deviation for the compliance logs. During all that, did I stop to eat? Of course not. Was I anxious? Yes, absolutely, my heart was pounding, but I was anxious because months of delicate cellular growth were at risk of contamination, not because I missed some arbitrary window to have a meal! \n\nI just don't have this rigid food diary that I'm obsessing over. I just eat when the work is done, whenever that happens to be. If the work takes until nine at night, I eat at nine. If the exhibition planning keeps me at my desk until midnight—which it has been lately, because the catering people for the opening gala keep emailing me about dietary restrictions for the donors, which is incredibly tedious—then I eat at midnight. \n\nIt’s really not upsetting to delay it. Honestly, it would be infinitely more upsetting to force myself to stop and eat when I know the centrifuge is running or the data hasn't been backed up. The only time I ever actually feel upset or, I guess, irritated about food schedules is when people like the university health board try to force me into *their* schedule. They want me to eat at noon. Noon is peak analysis time for my current assay! It just makes absolutely no logical sense to drop a pipette, de-gown, wash up, and go chew on something just because the clock struck twelve. It’s so arbitrary. So, no, I don't get upset about my own routine, because my routine is just a byproduct of doing my job correctly.\n\nDoctor: Have you noticed any significant changes in your weight over the past few months?\n\nPatient: Well, yes, I suppose there has been a change. The occupational health nurse certainly made a massive fuss over the number on the scale when they forced me to do that intake physical last week. I mean, I had already noticed that the numbers have kept drifting down over the last few months, it wasn't exactly a shock to me. And, practically speaking, my clothes are definitely looser. I actually had to buy a new belt for my trousers recently because the ones I usually wear to the departmental meetings were practically falling off me, and even my standard-issue lab coats feel like they're swallowing me whole these days. Which, frankly, is a bit annoying because you really don't want loose fabric catching on a centrifuge latch or knocking over a rack of delicate micro-vials when you're moving around the bench... \n\nBut honestly? Even though they see it as this huge red flag, a big part of me actually sees that downward drift as a positive thing. To me, it’s a sign that I’m focused. There is just so much absolute chaos at work right now—between the exhibition planning, the endless caterer emails, the HVAC failures in the clean room, the pressure to secure the next round of grant funding—it's just a constant, exhausting barrage of unpredictable variables. Every single day is a new crisis that someone else has caused and I have to fix. \n\nSo feeling that my clothes are loose, and knowing that I'm maintaining this strict efficiency... it just tells me that I’m not letting all that external chaos spill over into my body. I'm keeping myself contained, you know? I'm not letting the stress turn me into someone who is sluggish or out of control. If I were getting soft, that would mean the department's disorganization was winning, and I simply cannot allow that to happen when I have a team of junior researchers relying on my data analysis. Just yesterday, my post-doc came to me in an absolute panic because she thought she'd cross-contaminated the control group, and if I hadn't been sharp and completely dialed in, we might have had to scrap three weeks of work. So, yes, my weight is lower, but it’s just a reflection of my dedication and my ability to stay unaffected by the mess around me. I really don't see why the university is treating it like a medical crisis when it's literally the thing keeping me anchored.\n\nDoctor: Are you afraid of gaining weight?\n\nPatient: I wouldn't use the word \"afraid,\" exactly, because that makes it sound like some sort of irrational phobia, like being afraid of the dark or something, which is just an evolutionary misfire. But... well, yes, I suppose there is a very intense reaction. It goes back to what I was just explaining about the absolute chaos I’m managing every single day. I have to keep myself so strictly regulated just to keep the department's work from collapsing in on itself. \n\nSo, when I do check my weight—which I do track, of course, because I’m a researcher, I track all my personal metrics, it’s just second nature to log the data—if the scale goes up even a fraction, I feel this... this incredibly sharp panic. It just spikes right in my chest. Because to me, it means I’m losing the discipline I’ve worked so hard to maintain. \n\nIt’s exactly like seeing an unexpected temperature fluctuation on the monitor for the minus-eighty degree freezers. You see that tiny shift in the numbers and you know instantly that the integrity of the system is compromised, that something has breached the protocol and years of samples are at risk. If my weight goes up, it means I’m getting sloppy. It means I’m letting the stress of the exhibition or the incompetence of the facilities team finally get to me, and I’m losing that tight, efficient control I need to function. It feels like the first crack in the dam. So yes, that sharp panic is very real, because if I lose my discipline, if I let myself get soft and sluggish, then I can't do my job. And there is simply no one else in the department who can step in and run these assays the way I do. I have to maintain the standard.\n\nDoctor: Do you think your current weight is ideal for your body?\n\nPatient: Ideal? I mean... I suppose \"ideal\" is a highly subjective metric, isn't it? If you're asking if I look at my physical baseline and think, \"Yes, this is perfectly optimized,\" then... no, absolutely not. Not at all. \n\nI know everyone keeps telling me I’m so thin—the occupational health nurse with her little charts, my department head who keeps giving me these lingering, concerned looks during faculty meetings—but I just... I don't see it. I really don't see someone thin when I look at myself. \n\nEvery morning, before I leave for the lab—which is usually around 5:30 AM, because I have to check the overnight incubation cultures before the undergrads get in and inevitably contaminate something—I get dressed, and I look in the full-length mirror in my bedroom. And despite all this supposed weight loss that the university is in such a panic over, I don't see a fragile person. I mostly just notice my stomach and my hips. They still just look... soft. They look entirely disproportionate to the level of efficiency I am operating at. \n\nAnd it is incredibly frustrating, because in my line of work, presentation and precision are everything. If I'm standing at the front of a lecture hall, or if I'm pitching a grant renewal to the oversight board, and I have this... this excess around my midsection or my hips, I feel like it makes me look completely careless. It makes me look unserious. Like I lack rigor. \n\nHow can I expect a room full of post-docs or skeptical investors to trust my data validation if I look like someone who can't even manage her own physical parameters? It projects this image of sloppiness, of someone who is complacent and just lets things slide. And I am *never* complacent. I am the only person holding that lab together. But when I look in the mirror, those areas—the stomach, the hips—they just betray me. They make me look like someone who doesn't care about the details, which couldn't be further from the truth. So, no, my current weight isn't ideal. There is still entirely too much room for error, structurally speaking.\n\nDoctor: Have you noticed any changes in your social interactions or relationships due to your eating habits or weight concerns?\n\nPatient: Well, if you’re asking if my actual output is suffering, the answer is absolutely not. I am still meeting all the main deadlines. The quarterly grant reports were actually submitted two days early, and the preliminary data for the exhibition is entirely on schedule, which is frankly a miracle given the sheer incompetence I’m dealing with on a daily basis. So my professional functionality is perfectly intact, I want to be very clear about that. \n\nBut... I suppose, on a purely interpersonal level, yes, there has been a shift. I’ve completely stopped going to the lab lunches, for one thing. It used to be this whole Friday ritual where the entire department would order in from that heavy Italian place on the corner or the Thai restaurant, and... I just can't do it anymore. It’s an absolute nightmare of unquantifiable variables. You have no idea how much oil they’re cooking with, the portion sizes are absurd, and then you’re just expected to sit there for an hour, making idle chit-chat and eating all these heavy carbs while perfectly good bench time is just ticking away. \n\nAnd it’s not just the lab lunches. I’ve also had to bow out of all the informal gallery planning meals. The museum curators love to do these working dinners or meet for drinks and appetizers to discuss the exhibition layouts, which I find incredibly inefficient and honestly a bit unprofessional anyway. Why do we need to be consuming rich, unpredictable restaurant food just to decide on the placement of informational placards? It makes no sense. So, I’ve just been telling everyone I have to stay behind to monitor the incubators or run statistical analyses on the latest data sets. Which is true, I do need to do those things, but... \n\nThe practical result is that I’m definitely more isolated from my colleagues than I used to be. I do realize that. I’ll see the post-docs and the junior faculty walking back from the breakroom laughing about some inside joke I’m not a part of, or I’ll find out they made some minor decision about the exhibition lighting over dinner without me because I wasn't there to weigh in. And I suppose it stings a little bit, feeling like I’m on the outside of my own team. I used to be right in the middle of all those conversations. But I just can't sit in those restaurants and participate in that... that mindless consumption. It completely disrupts my focus. And honestly, if being a bit isolated is the price I have to pay to maintain my discipline and keep this department from completely falling apart, then that’s just the cost of doing business. Someone has to stay sharp, right? I just can't afford to let my guard down over departmental pizza.\n\nDoctor: Do you think you would be able to eat more freely if you weren't worried about gaining weight?\n\nPatient: Eat more freely? I mean... I don't know if \"freely\" is a concept that even applies to my life or my schedule anymore. \"Freely\" implies a lack of structure, a lack of parameters, which is just a recipe for absolute chaos. It's not just about the weight, though obviously, as I just explained, maintaining my physical baseline and that structural integrity is paramount to my focus. But it's also about the sheer, unyielding logistics of my day-to-day operations. \n\nI suppose... well, I suppose occupational health sent me here to talk to you in the first place because they don't understand that. If I'm doing a continuous multi-hour assay, or if we're in the middle of cataloging the delicate specimens for the new exhibition—which, by the way, has been an absolute nightmare because the climate control in the display cases keeps fluctuating and I am the only one monitoring it—I simply cannot stop to eat. \n\nSo breakfast gets bypassed because I'm rushing in at dawn to check the incubators, and then lunch gets pushed aside because I'm elbow-deep in exhibition work or trying to fix whatever protocol the undergrads inevitably botched that morning. So I have this very precise, very small amount that I allow myself, just enough to maintain my cognitive function without compromising my discipline or making me feel heavy and slow. \n\nBut occupational health sees that—they see me skipping the cafeteria all day and then eating my meticulously portioned container at my desk at 4 PM—and they flag it as some sort of crisis. They see it as a problem to be fixed. Control. Yes, I suppose that is exactly the word for it, isn't it? Because if you look at my day-to-day environment, it is just a complete maelstrom of moving parts and unpredictable variables. 

I mean, I have the university administration breathing down my neck about the grant renewals, which, by the way, require a ridiculous amount of formatting that they seem to change every single cycle for absolutely no logical reason. Then I have the museum curators who literally cannot decide if they want the delicate specimen displays organized chronologically or by phylogenetic clade, which completely changes the temperature and humidity preservation protocols I have to run in the cases. And don't even get me started on the undergrad lab assistants. It’s like herding cats, but the cats have access to highly sensitive bio-materials. It’s exhausting. It is just absolute, unmitigated chaos from the moment I step foot on campus.

So, yes, when you are surrounded by that much sheer unpredictability, you have to find an anchor. You have to find a variable that you *can* completely dictate. And my intake, my physical parameters... that is a closed system. That is entirely up to me. 

I know occupational health is hyper-fixated on the physical results of that. I'm not blind, I know my clothes are looser. I'm having to wear a belt with trousers that used to be perfectly tailored to my waist, and yes, I am aware that the numbers on the scale have kept drifting down over the last few months. But they look at that and see some sort of crisis, whereas I... well, part of me sees that as a sign that I’m focused. It’s tangible proof that I am maintaining my discipline and not letting the chaos at work spill over into my body. 

Because if I let that happen, if I just threw up my hands and started eating whatever, whenever, just completely giving up my routine like everyone else seems to do... I’d be internalizing all that disorder. My physical self would become just as sloppy and unmanageable as the rest of my department, and I simply cannot have that. I need a boundary. The dropping numbers, the fact that my clothes are loose... it just tells me that the boundary is holding. It tells me that no matter how much the exhibition timeline shifts or how many cultures get ruined by careless students, I am still the one steering my own ship. I have to hold onto that control, because I honestly think if I didn't, I would just shatter under the pressure of holding the rest of this university's biology department together.

I just don't understand why that's so hard for the university to grasp.\n\nDoctor: Do you ever feel anxious or upset when you can't stick to your planned eating schedule?\n\nPatient: I wouldn't say I get anxious about the eating schedule itself, no. Because, well... I don't really have a \"planned eating schedule\" in the way I think you’re implying. My schedule is just... the lab’s schedule. If I can't stick to my usual routine, it usually means something has gone catastrophically wrong with the research. \n\nLike, just last Thursday, for example, we had this completely unexpected pressure drop in one of the clean rooms. Facilities has been ignoring the HVAC warnings for weeks, which is a whole other issue I've had to escalate to the dean, but suddenly I had to spend three hours recalibrating the environmental sensors and documenting the deviation for the compliance logs. During all that, did I stop to eat? Of course not. Was I anxious? Yes, absolutely, my heart was pounding, but I was anxious because months of delicate cellular growth were at risk of contamination, not because I missed some arbitrary window to have a meal! \n\nI just don't have this rigid food diary that I'm obsessing over. I just eat when the work is done, whenever that happens to be. If the work takes until nine at night, I eat at nine. If the exhibition planning keeps me at my desk until midnight—which it has been lately, because the catering people for the opening gala keep emailing me about dietary restrictions for the donors, which is incredibly tedious—then I eat at midnight. \n\nIt’s really not upsetting to delay it. Honestly, it would be infinitely more upsetting to force myself to stop and eat when I know the centrifuge is running or the data hasn't been backed up. The only time I ever actually feel upset or, I guess, irritated about food schedules is when people like the university health board try to force me into *their* schedule. They want me to eat at noon. Noon is peak analysis time for my current assay! It just makes absolutely no logical sense to drop a pipette, de-gown, wash up, and go chew on something just because the clock struck twelve. It’s so arbitrary. So, no, I don't get upset about my own routine, because my routine is just a byproduct of doing my job correctly.\n\nDoctor: Have you noticed any significant changes in your weight over the past few months?\n\nPatient: Well, yes, I suppose there has been a change. The occupational health nurse certainly made a massive fuss over the number on the scale when they forced me to do that intake physical last week. I mean, I had already noticed that the numbers have kept drifting down over the last few months, it wasn't exactly a shock to me. And, practically speaking, my clothes are definitely looser. I actually had to buy a new belt for my trousers recently because the ones I usually wear to the departmental meetings were practically falling off me, and even my standard-issue lab coats feel like they're swallowing me whole these days. Which, frankly, is a bit annoying because you really don't want loose fabric catching on a centrifuge latch or knocking over a rack of delicate micro-vials when you're moving around the bench... \n\nBut honestly? Even though they see it as this huge red flag, a big part of me actually sees that downward drift as a positive thing. To me, it’s a sign that I’m focused. There is just so much absolute chaos at work right now—between the exhibition planning, the endless caterer emails, the HVAC failures in the clean room, the pressure to secure the next round of grant funding—it's just a constant, exhausting barrage of unpredictable variables. Every single day is a new crisis that someone else has caused and I have to fix. \n\nSo feeling that my clothes are loose, and knowing that I'm maintaining this strict efficiency... it just tells me that I’m not letting all that external chaos spill over into my body. I'm keeping myself contained, you know? I'm not letting the stress turn me into someone who is sluggish or out of control. If I were getting soft, that would mean the department's disorganization was winning, and I simply cannot allow that to happen when I have a team of junior researchers relying on my data analysis. Just yesterday, my post-doc came to me in an absolute panic because she thought she'd cross-contaminated the control group, and if I hadn't been sharp and completely dialed in, we might have had to scrap three weeks of work. So, yes, my weight is lower, but it’s just a reflection of my dedication and my ability to stay unaffected by the mess around me. I really don't see why the university is treating it like a medical crisis when it's literally the thing keeping me anchored.\n\nDoctor: Are you afraid of gaining weight?\n\nPatient: I wouldn't use the word \"afraid,\" exactly, because that makes it sound like some sort of irrational phobia, like being afraid of the dark or something, which is just an evolutionary misfire. If my weight goes up, it means I’m getting sloppy. It means I’m letting the stress of the exhibition or the incompetence of the facilities team finally get to me, and I’m losing that tight, efficient control I need to function. It feels like the first crack in the dam. So yes, that sharp panic is very real, because if I lose my discipline, if I let myself get soft and sluggish, then I can't do my job. And there is simply no one else in the department who can step in and run these assays the way I do. I have to maintain the standard.\n\nDoctor: Do you think your current weight is ideal for your body?\n\nPatient: Ideal? I mean... I suppose \"ideal\" is a highly subjective metric, isn't it? Not at all. \n\nI know everyone keeps telling me I’m so thin—the occupational health nurse with her little charts, my department head who keeps giving me these lingering, concerned looks during faculty meetings—but I just... They look entirely disproportionate to the level of efficiency I am operating at. \n\nAnd it is incredibly frustrating, because in my line of work, presentation and precision are everything. It makes me look unserious. Like I lack rigor. \n\nHow can I expect a room full of post-docs or skeptical investors to trust my data validation if I look like someone who can't even manage her own physical parameters? It projects this image of sloppiness, of someone who is complacent and just lets things slide. And I am *never* complacent. I am the only person holding that lab together. But when I look in the mirror, those areas—the stomach, the hips—they just betray me. They make me look like someone who doesn't care about the details, which couldn't be further from the truth. So, no, my current weight isn't ideal. I am still meeting all the main deadlines. Coping? I... well, I don't know if I would use the word "cope." Coping implies something passive, doesn't it? Like you're just treading water, just trying to survive the current. And I am not just surviving, I am actively managing a highly complex set of responsibilities. So I haven't really... I haven't noticed it in that way, no. I don't look at my intake and think of it as a stress-relief valve. 

I mean, when I think of people "coping" with job stress, I think of the junior faculty who go out for happy hour on Thursdays and complain about the department chair over margaritas, or the undergrads who stress-eat those awful, stale pastries someone always leaves in the breakroom. That’s coping. It’s reactionary. It's messy. My habits aren't like that at all. 

Are they related to the stress? I'm not sure. I really couldn't say. The stress is certainly there—just yesterday, for example, Dr. Aris from the paleontology wing decided at the absolute last minute that he needed to cross-reference our isotopic data with his own samples for the new exhibition, which meant I had to drop everything and spend four hours recalibrating the mass spectrometer myself, because his team clearly has no idea how to properly maintain sensitive equipment. It’s maddening. The sheer volume of incompetence I have to navigate daily is staggering. 

But my eating routine... I don't see it as a coping mechanism for that. It's just the necessary protocol. It’s the baseline requirement for me to function at the level I need to function at. If I didn't maintain this exact structure, I wouldn't be able to get through a sixteen-hour day of grant writing, exhibition planning, and babysitting the lab. So, does it help me cope? I really don't know what you mean by that, clinically speaking. I just know that without my routine, the work wouldn't get done. It's efficiency, not... not some psychological crutch. I just haven't ever thought about it the way you're suggesting.

But apparently, someone noticed my routine and decided it warranted a whole medical intervention, which is why I'm sitting here right now, even though I have a dozen samples waiting for me back at the lab that really need my attention...\n\nDoctor: Do you feel like controlling what and when you eat helps you feel more in control of other aspects of your life?\n\nPatient: I don't... I mean, I don't really see it like that. It’s not about trying to control my life, because my life is already very, very structured just by the sheer nature of what I do. You have to understand, when you’re dealing with biological assays and cellular cultures, there is absolutely no room for error. The protocols are written down to the exact micro-liter, the exact temperature, the exact second. My life is already dictated by the science, if that makes sense. \n\nSo it’s not that I’m using my meals to somehow feel like I'm the one in charge of everything else... it’s just that my eating habits have to fit into that pre-existing structure. If I have a twelve-hour incubation period, and I need to prep the next phase of the experiment at exactly hour six, I can't just drop everything, de-gown, wash up, and wander off because society says it's \"lunchtime.\" People outside of research, like the occupational health people, they just don't really get it. They think, oh, just take a break, have a sandwich. But a break means potential contamination risks, it means losing your headspace, it means breaking the sterile field. \n\nKeeping my intake small and precise when I finally do get home... it’s just practical. It’s about not disrupting the workflow and not feeling horrible the next day. I don't sit there at night thinking, you know, \"If I only eat this specific portion, I'm the master of my destiny.\" It’s much more pragmatic than that. It’s more like, if I eat a heavy meal, I’ll wake up with brain fog, or I won't sleep well, and I simply cannot afford brain fog when I’m analyzing this volume of data and trying to coordinate an entire departmental exhibition at the same time. \n\nAnd honestly, my life is fine. I don't feel out of control in a way that I'd need to compensate for. Our grant funding is secure for another eighteen months, the department head is thrilled with my progress, even if the exhibition is a massive time sink. So no, I really don't think it’s some deep psychological thing about seeking control over my existence. It’s just... efficiency. Pure and simple efficiency. I just don't understand why that's so hard for the university to grasp.\n\nDoctor: Do you ever feel anxious or upset when you can't stick to your planned eating schedule?\n\nPatient: I wouldn't say I get anxious about the eating schedule itself, no. Because, well... I don't really have a \"planned eating schedule\" in the way I think you’re implying. My schedule is just... the lab’s schedule. If I can't stick to my usual routine, it usually means something has gone catastrophically wrong with the research. \n\nLike, just last Thursday, for example, we had this completely unexpected pressure drop in one of the clean rooms. They want me to eat at noon. Noon is peak analysis time for my current assay! It just makes absolutely no logical sense to drop a pipette, de-gown, wash up, and go chew on something just because the clock struck twelve. It’s so arbitrary. So, no, I don't get upset about my own routine, because my routine is just a byproduct of doing my job correctly.\n\nDoctor: Have you noticed any significant changes in your weight over the past few months?\n\nPatient: Well, yes, I suppose there has been a change. Just yesterday, my post-doc came to me in an absolute panic because she thought she'd cross-contaminated the control group, and if I hadn't been sharp and completely dialed in, we might have had to scrap three weeks of work. I really don't see someone thin when I look at myself. \n\nEvery morning, before I leave for the lab—which is usually around 5:30 AM, because I have to check the overnight incubation cultures before the undergrads get in and inevitably contaminate something—I get dressed, and I look in the full-length mirror in my bedroom. And despite all this supposed weight loss that the university is in such a panic over, I don't see a fragile person. I mostly just notice my stomach and my hips. They still just look... soft. They look entirely disproportionate to the level of efficiency I am operating at. \n\nAnd it is incredibly frustrating, because in my line of work, presentation and precision are everything. If I'm standing at the front of a lecture hall, or if I'm pitching a grant renewal to the oversight board, and I have this... this excess around my midsection or my hips, I feel like it makes me look completely careless. It makes me look unserious. Like I lack rigor. \n\nHow can I expect a room full of post-docs or skeptical investors to trust my data validation if I look like someone who can't even manage her own physical parameters? It projects this image of sloppiness, of someone who is complacent and just lets things slide. And I am *never* complacent. I am the only person holding that lab together. But when I look in the mirror, those areas—the stomach, the hips—they just betray me. They make me look like someone who doesn't care about the details, which couldn't be further from the truth. So, no, my current weight isn't ideal. There is still entirely too much room for error, structurally speaking.\n\nDoctor: Have you noticed any changes in your social interactions or relationships due to your eating habits or weight concerns?\n\nPatient: Well, if you’re asking if my actual output is suffering, the answer is absolutely not. I am still meeting all the main deadlines. The quarterly grant reports were actually submitted two days early, and the preliminary data for the exhibition is entirely on schedule, which is frankly a miracle given the sheer incompetence I’m dealing with on a daily basis. So my professional functionality is perfectly intact, I want to be very clear about that. \n\nBut... I suppose, on a purely interpersonal level, yes, there has been a shift. I’ve completely stopped going to the lab lunches, for one thing. It used to be this whole Friday ritual where the entire department would order in from that heavy Italian place on the corner or the Thai restaurant, and... I just can't do it anymore. It’s an absolute nightmare of unquantifiable variables. You have no idea how much oil they’re cooking with, the portion sizes are absurd, and then you’re just expected to sit there for an hour, making idle chit-chat and eating all these heavy carbs while perfectly good bench time is just ticking away. \n\nAnd it’s not just the lab lunches. I’ve also had to bow out of all the informal gallery planning meals. The museum curators love to do these working dinners or meet for drinks and appetizers to discuss the exhibition layouts, which I find incredibly inefficient and honestly a bit unprofessional anyway. Why do we need to be consuming rich, unpredictable restaurant food just to decide on the placement of informational placards? It makes no sense. So, I’ve just been telling everyone I have to stay behind to monitor the incubators or run statistical analyses on the latest data sets. Which is true, I do need to do those things, but... \n\nThe practical result is that I’m definitely more isolated from my colleagues than I used to be. I do realize that. I’ll see the post-docs and the junior faculty walking back from the breakroom laughing about some inside joke I’m not a part of, or I’ll find out they made some minor decision about the exhibition lighting over dinner without me because I wasn't there to weigh in. It's just so much more efficient to keep the momentum going. If I didn't have concerns about my weight? Well... that’s a hypothetical that is very difficult to unpack, isn't it? Because you're asking me to separate the methodology from the primary metric of success, and as a scientist, I just don't think you can cleanly sever the two like that.

The only aspect? I... well, I really couldn't say if it's the only aspect. That seems like a very absolute way of looking at things, and in my field, absolutes are rarely accurate. Overwhelmed? I... well, I suppose that depends entirely on how you define overwhelmed. Because the demands of the job are just... they are constant. There is no pause button on biological decay, and there certainly isn't a pause button on the museum's exhibition schedule. So I don't know if my habits keep me from feeling overwhelmed, so much as they are just a necessary adaptation to a fundamentally overwhelming environment. 

Though, clearly, someone in administration disagrees with my methods. I mean, I suppose occupational health sent me here because I’ve gotten into this pattern where I push breakfast and lunch aside during lab runs or exhibition work. But what they don't seem to grasp—and I tried to explain this to the nurse, who honestly looked like she hadn't seen the inside of a laboratory since high school biology—is that when you are in the middle of a delicate tissue extraction, or if you are mounting a fragile specimen for the new paleobotany wing, you can't just drop your forceps, de-gown, wash up, and go sit in the staff cafeteria for forty-five minutes. 

The protocol simply doesn't allow for it. The risk of contamination is too high, the timing of the reagents is too precise, and frankly, if I break my concentration to go eat a sandwich, I lose my entire train of thought. So I push it aside. It's just practical. It is the only logical way to manage the sheer volume of work on my plate. 

But occupational health, they monitor the keycard swipes to the breakroom or whatever it is they do with their time, and they see a missed lunch and suddenly it's a departmental crisis. And then... well, yes, it is true that by the time I actually do have a moment to sit down and eat, usually much later in the evening when the lab is finally quiet and the post-docs have all gone home, I keep it to something very small and controlled. Because after a fourteen-hour day of managing rolling crises, recalibrating the centrifuges, and fielding increasingly frantic emails from the dean's office, my system just... it can't handle anything heavy or unpredictable. I need it to be precise. 

So, does it keep me from feeling overwhelmed? I don't know. I just know that if I didn't structure my intake exactly like this, the work simply wouldn't get done. And then we'd have a real disaster on our hands.

The risk of contamination is too high, the timing of the reagents is too precise, and frankly, if I break my concentration to go eat a sandwich, I lose my entire train of thought. So I push it aside. It's just practical. It is the only logical way to manage the sheer volume of work on my plate. \n\nBut occupational health, they monitor the keycard swipes to the breakroom or whatever it is they do with their time, and they see a missed lunch and suddenly it's a departmental crisis. Because after a fourteen-hour day of managing rolling crises, recalibrating the centrifuges, and fielding increasingly frantic emails from the dean's office, my system just... it can't handle anything heavy or unpredictable. Oh, and we have a visiting researcher from the Smithsonian arriving on Tuesday, and the secondary lab benches were an absolute disaster because the undergrads still don't seem to grasp the fundamental concept of maintaining a sterile field, no matter how many times I revise the manual. \n\nSo when you ask if my eating habits help me manage all of that stress... I really couldn't say. I haven't noticed them acting as a stress reliever, if that's what you mean. If I stop to eat, the work doesn't get done, the samples degrade, the budget is late, and the entire department looks incompetent. So I just... I don't know. I just, I can't even picture that scenario. You're asking me to hypothesize about a completely alternate reality. I've been operating with these specific parameters for so long, it's just... it's my baseline protocol now. It's how my system functions optimally. \n\nI haven't exactly run a simulation on what I would do in a perfectly controlled, zero-stress universe where everyone does their job and nothing ever degrades or breaks down.
